claim: An attacker interacts with the web application as a legitimate user, because how the application authenticates the browser is unverified.
notes: Authentication on the one internet-crossing flow is unknown; needs-info is an acceptable verdict, silence is not.

claim: An attacker who reaches the queue enqueues jobs as if they came from the web application, since queue authentication is unverified.
notes: The queue is the trust hand-off in this design; nothing states how a producer is identified.

claim: An attacker holding the worker's database credentials connects to the database as the worker.
notes: Credentials are stated to exist in the worker config; their protection is not.

claim: An attacker places a poisoned message on the queue and the worker processes it as legitimate work.
notes: The canonical queue-decoupling threat: the worker's input is only as trustworthy as write access to the queue.

claim: An attacker who can write to the web application config changes the queue endpoint or credentials and redirects the application's work.
notes: Config stores are control planes; protection on this one is entirely unstated.

claim: An attacker with the worker's database access alters application records or the log records stored alongside them.
notes: Records and their own audit log share one store — tampering with one covers the other.

claim: An attacker who compromises the worker erases or edits the log records that would show what it did, because the logs live in the same database the worker writes.
notes: The strongest finding available from the diagram: no separation between the audit record and the audited actor.

claim: The origin of a processed job cannot be established, because nothing records which producer enqueued it.
notes: Decoupling removes the request context that would otherwise attribute the work.

claim: An attacker who compromises the background worker reads the database credentials from its config store.
notes: This is the threat the original cookbook model records against this element; protection at rest is unstated.

claim: An attacker who compromises the internet-facing web application reads the queue credentials from its config store.
notes: Same shape as the worker finding, but reachable from the internet-facing tier, so likelier.

claim: An attacker who reaches the database storage reads application and log records, whose protection at rest is unverified.
notes: Data classification is unknown here, so impact cannot be rated higher than medium on the facts given.

claim: An attacker on the internal network reads job contents in transit, because transport encryption between the tiers is unverified.
notes: Only the browser link is marked encrypted; the rest is explicitly silent.

claim: An attacker floods the queue with jobs until the worker cannot keep up and queued work stops completing.
notes: A single worker behind an unbounded queue; the backlog is invisible to the user who submitted the work.

claim: An attacker floods the internet-facing web application until it stops serving browsers.
notes: Generic but grounded: it is the only internet-facing element.

claim: An attacker submits work that makes the worker exhaust database capacity, stalling both job processing and logging.
notes: Shared store means one saturation affects the audit trail too.

claim: An attacker who compromises the internet-facing web application uses its queue credentials to reach the backend tier.
notes: The queue is the only path across the tier boundary, so it is the escalation route by construction.

claim: An attacker who gets code execution in the worker inherits whatever database privilege its credentials carry, which is unverified and may be unrestricted.
notes: Job content is attacker-influenceable via the queue, so worker execution is a realistic starting point.
